quote: Two adjacent parts should be shown with lines at 45° and in opposite directions. The third part adjacent to the first two should have lines at 30° or 60°.

rule: A local (partial) section is bounded by a thick, irregular, freehand break line.
note: The lines table on pdf 67R labels break lines medium; this page says thick. Line-weight checks are deferred.
quote: A local section may be drawn if a full or a half section is not necessary ... the local break is shown by a thick, irregular, free-hand break line.

rule: Shafts, bolts, nuts, rods, rivets, keys, pins, pulley arms and similar parts are shown unsectioned when the cutting plane runs along them, and ribs and webs cut lengthwise are not hatched.
note: same rule as VW-09. Same as VW-09; relevant to round parts drawn in section.
quote: Section plane through pulley arms, shafts, bolts, nuts, rods, rivets, keys, pins ... shown by normal unsectioned views ... rib or web cross-hatching should be eliminated.

rule: Each cutting plane is labelled with capital letters and has arrows resting on the cutting line that show the viewing direction.
note: adds detail to VW-003. Letters come from the text layer, arrows from vectors. The cutting-plane line style itself is in WST-014.
quote: They are designated by capital letters, the direction of viewing being shown by arrows resting on the cutting line.

rule: A cross-section revolved in place is outlined in continuous thick lines and needs no label, so the section-label check does not flag it, while removed sections are identified.
note: adds detail to VW-003. Exception to VW-003. Telling a revolved section from a removed one needs the vision summary. That removed sections are labelled is implied by contrast, not stated. The book spells indentification.
quote: Cross sections may be revolved in place (A) or removed (B). In the first case, the outline is shown in continuous thick lines and further indentification is not necessary.

rule: In a section through a part with an odd number of spokes, ribs or holes, the inclined or unsymmetrical elements are rotated into the plane of the paper instead of being drawn in true projection.
note: Common on round flanges with three equally spaced holes. A vision-based warning may become possible later.
quote: Any part having odd numbers of spokes, ribs or holes will give an unsymmetrical and misleading section ... those inclined elements ... should be rotated into the plane of paper.

rule: When a symmetrical part is drawn as a half or other fraction of the whole, its line of symmetry is marked by two short parallel strokes at each end, perpendicular to it.
quote: A line of symmetry is identified by two short parallel strokes drawn at each end and perpendicular to it.

rule: Adjacent parts shown for reference are drawn in thin long-dash-and-dot lines, do not hide the part being drawn, and are hatched only along their outlines when needed to avoid confusion.
note: adds detail to LY-01. The book uses a single-dot chain; the PARI template may use another phantom line. Single-part PARI drawings sometimes show mating parts.
quote: parts adjacent to an object are drawn by a thin line made up of alternate long dash and dot. The adjacent part should not hide the principal part

rule: A shortened (interrupted) view of a solid bar or a tube is shown with the conventional break for that section.
note: same rule as VW-13. VW-13 (phase2_3d) also wants true-length dimensions; this is the representation only.
quote: A. Interrupted view of solid bar. B. Interrupted view of tube.

rule: Screw threads are drawn in the conventional representation shown for external and internal threads, in plain view and in section.
note: Also on pdf 69R: C. External threads in section. D. Internal threads in section. CAD generates the representation, so this is mostly a sanity check.
quote: Internal thread ... External thread

rule: Every dimension and tolerance needed for the part to function is stated directly, so no functional dimension has to be deduced from others or scaled from the drawing.
note: same rule as ISO-012. Also supports MX-07 (implied dimension) and MX-001/MX-002. The same paragraph asks for everything needed to define the part completely in its finished form.
quote: It should not be necessary to deduce a functional dimension from other dimensions or to scale the drawing.

rule: Dimension values are written either in a gap left in the dimension line or above the dimension line.
note: adds detail to ISO-32. The gap style is the ASME habit and above-the-line is ISO; the PARI choice is open. A v1 check could compare text position with the dimension-line vector.
quote: the amount of which is denoted by figures in a space left in the dimension line or above the dimension line.

rule: Extension lines start about 2 mm clear of the outline and extend about 3 mm beyond the dimension line.
note: adds detail to DTT-18. CONFLICT with DTT-18, which says about 1 mm past the last dimension line.
quote: There should be a gap of about 2 mm outside the outline and the line should extend about 3 mm beyond the dimensioning line.

rule: Extension lines are thin and perpendicular to the outline; where they have to be oblique they are kept parallel to each other.
note: same rule as ISO-18.
quote: Extension lines (projection lines) are light full lines extending perpendicular to outline ... They could be oblique where necessary but preferably parallel to each other.

rule: Arrowheads are filled in and about three times as long as they are wide; where space is limited, adjacent arrowheads may be replaced by clearly marked dots.
note: adds detail to ISO-025. Arrowheads are vector polygons, so the ratio is measurable, but the Solid Edge dimension style fixes it. ISO-025 (v1) covers using one style and dots in tight spaces.
quote: Its length is about three times the depth and the space should be filled in. Adjacent arrow-heads may be replaced by clearly marked dots where space is limited.

rule: Where space between extension lines is limited, the arrowheads are reversed to sit outside them.
note: same rule as ISO-26.
quote: For dimensioning in limited space, the arrow-heads should be reversed.

rule: On several parallel dimension lines the values are staggered rather than stacked directly above one another.
note: Measurable from text positions, but it is a layout-quality check like VW-06.
quote: When there are several parallel dimension lines the figures should be staggered to avoid confusion.

rule: Leaders are thin straight lines ending in an arrowhead on a line or a dot inside the outline, and the note end may finish in a short horizontal bar at mid-height of the first or last line of the note.
note: adds detail to NASA-065. The page also prints: The leader should be curved or made free hand. This is almost certainly a misprint for should not be; the figures show straight leaders. Not used in the requirement.
quote: These are thin straight lines terminated by arrow-heads or dots. Arrow-heads should always terminate on a line; dots should be within the outline of the object.

rule: Dimension values follow one of the two recommended placement systems, aligned or unidirectional.
note: same rule as ISO-030. The book does not pick one; ISO-030 adds one method throughout. DSM-22 and DTT-26 (needs_pari) prefer unidirectional.
quote: The two recommended systems of placing the dimensions are: (a) Aligned system (b) Unidirectional system

rule: Every radius dimension carries the letter R with its value.
note: same rule as DTT-007. The book writes R after the value (10R); DTT-007 wants it before (R10). The position question is WST-046.
quote: should be followed by the letter R ... 5R ... 3R ... 10R

rule: The letter R and the diameter symbol ϕ are written after the value (10R, 50ϕ, 30ϕ Sphere), as this book shows.
note: Obsolete notation: PARI's drawings and Solid Edge write R10 and Ø50, symbol first (DTT-007). CONFLICTS with DTT-007 (symbol before the value). Solid Edge and current ISO practice write R10, Ø50, SØ30. Once PARI confirms, the checker should accept its style and could flag a mix of both.
quote: should be followed by the letter R ... 10R ... 50ϕ ... 125ϕ ... 30ϕSphere

rule: Small radii are dimensioned from outside the outline of the part where possible.
note: same rule as DSM-17.
quote: Wherever possible, the dimensions of small radii should be shown outside the outline of the object

rule: Where the centre of a radius is located by dimensions, a dot marks the centre at the intersection of the locating lines.
note: Related to MP-11 (centre of a large arc is located).
quote: Where the centre point of a radius is dimensioned, a dot should be placed at the intersection of the lines which locate the centre of the radius.

rule: When an arc's centre cannot conveniently be shown in its true position, the radius dimension line is foreshortened (jogged), with the part touching the arc in line with the true centre.
quote: The portion of the dimension line which touches the arc should be in line with the true centre.

rule: Full circles are dimensioned by their diameter, using one of the illustrated methods (across the circle, by a leader or between extension lines), not by a radius.
source_document: Westermann Tables for the Metal Trade (Jutz-Scharkus), revised to Indian Standards; in PARI's WP Specific Guidelines (WESTERMANN_TABLES.pdf, a scan)
note: Every method shown gives a diameter (30, 20, 15, 10ϕ); not by a radius is inferred from that. Needs the closed circle vector linked to its dimension.
quote: The circles should be dimensioned by one of the methods illustrated here.

rule: A diameter dimensioned where it is not obvious, such as on the side view of a cylinder, or away from its circle, carries the diameter symbol.
note: adds detail to DTT-007. Key for round parts, whose diameters are dimensioned on the long view. DTT-007 wants Ø on every diameter; the book examples omit ϕ across a circle in its circular view, so the book is looser than DTT-007.
quote: Where it is not obvious that the dimension represents a diameter or where the dimension is remote from the circle, the use of the symbol ϕ is very essential.

rule: The diameter of a spherical surface is marked as a sphere (the book writes 30ϕ Sphere).
source_document: Westermann Tables for the Metal Trade (Jutz-Scharkus), revised to Indian Standards; in PARI's WP Specific Guidelines (WESTERMANN_TABLES.pdf, a scan)
note: Needs the vision summary to know the feature is spherical; the text check would accept SPHERE, SØ or SR. Notation is the old suffix style (see WST-046).
quote: The diameter of a spherical surface should be dimensioned as shown here. 30ϕSphere

rule: A tapered feature is fully defined by a suitable combination of end diameters or widths, length, a diameter at a located cross-section, and the taper rate (e.g. Taper 1:20) or included angle.
note: adds detail to MX-001. The vision summary identifies tapered features; the text layer gives the values.
quote: (a) Diameter (or width) at each end. (b) Length. (c) Diameter (or width) at a selected cross-sectional plane ... (e) The rate of taper or the included angle.

rule: Where a taper's end diameters, length and taper rate or angle are all given, they agree: (D − d) / L equals the stated taper rate and the angle matches.
note: Example: (40-35)/100 = 1:20; half angle atan(2.5/100) = 1°25.9', printed 1°25', so allow rounding to the minute. The book does not say whether the angle is the half or the included angle; the value fits the half angle. A taper given this many ways is also over-dimensioned (DM-002) unless some values are reference.

rule: A keyway is dimensioned by its width and by a depth taken across the section: in a shaft from the keyway bottom to the far side of the shaft, in a hub from the keyway bottom to the far side of the bore.
note: adds detail to MC-007. Read from the figures; no text. For tapered shafts and hubs the figures give the depth at the large end, and the Woodruff figures appear to give depth from the shaft surface [?]. Needs the vision summary to know what each dimension measures.
quote: Parallel hub ... Parallel shaft ... Tapered keyway in Parallel hub ... Parallel keyway in tapered shaft ... Woodruff keyway in parallel shaft

rule: A chamfer is dimensioned by its length and angle, either as separate dimensions or combined as length × angle (e.g. 6 × 45°).
source_document: Westermann Tables for the Metal Trade (Jutz-Scharkus), revised to Indian Standards; in PARI's WP Specific Guidelines (WESTERMANN_TABLES.pdf, a scan)
supporting_reference: related rule MX-001
note: In the figures the length (6) is measured along the axis. A chamfer with only an angle or only a length is incomplete. PARI writes length × angle ('0.5 X 45°' in the template's UNSP.CHF. field on 1,153 of 1,175 client PDFs), which passes.
quote: Dimensioning chamfers ... 45° ... 6 ... 6×45°

rule: When several parts are drawn in assembly, the dimensions of each part are kept in separate groups as far as possible.
note: Assembly drawings.
quote: When several parts are drawn in assembly, the groups of dimensions related to each part shall be kept separate as much as possible.

rule: Each dimension is given only once on the drawing.
note: same rule as DM-002.
quote: The dimensions should be quoted only once

rule: Each dimension is placed on the view that shows the feature most clearly, outside the views where possible and between views.
note: adds detail to DSM-17. DSM-17 says outside the outline; the book adds on the clearest view and between views.
quote: should be placed on the view which shows the relevant features most clearly. In general, dimensions should be placed outside of views where possible and between views.

rule: Dimensions are taken from visible outlines, not from hidden lines.
note: same rule as MX-10. Hidden lines are dashed vectors; linking extension lines to them is geometry work.
quote: Dimensions should be taken from visible outlines rather than from hidden lines.

rule: Dimensions are given from a base line, a centre line, an important hole or a finished surface that can be readily established according to the design requirements.
note: same rule as MD-11. Choosing the right origin needs the design intent. DTT-023 (v1) covers locating holes to their centre lines.
quote: They should be given from a base line, a centre line, an important hole or a finished surface which may be readily established according to the design requirements.

rule: No more dimensions are given than needed: when an overall dimension is shown, one intermediate distance of the chain is left out or shown in brackets.
note: same rule as DM-003. The figure shows the omitted link in brackets, (6), consistent with DM-010 (reference dimensions bracketed).
quote: More dimensions than necessary should be avoided. When an overall dimension is used, dimensioning of one intermediate distance may be left out.

rule: Where several dimensions share a common datum feature, they are given as parallel dimensions from that feature.
note: A layout preference like VW-06; as an LLM warning it would fire on most drawings that chain their dimensions, against the false-alarm target (M2). Should normally makes this a warning. Related to MP-012 (origin marked).
quote: Where a number of dimensions has a common datum feature, method shown here should normally be used.

rule: For equally spaced features dimensioned as number × pitch = total (e.g. 4 × 60 = 240, or 7 @ 75 = 525 in steelwork), the product equals the stated total.
source_document: Westermann Tables for the Metal Trade (Jutz-Scharkus), revised to Indian Standards; in PARI's WP Specific Guidelines (WESTERMANN_TABLES.pdf, a scan)
supporting_reference: related rule CN-001
note: Pure text-layer arithmetic. The figure chain also closes: 30 + 240 + 30 = 300 (CN-001). The @ form is from the structural example on pdf 73L.
quote: Where equidistant or regularly arranged elements appear on a drawing, the method shown here may be used for simplicity. 4×60=240

rule: Where the pitch could be confused with the number of pitches, one pitch is also dimensioned on its own.
note: adds detail to MX-006. Figure: 30, 60, 26×60=1560, 1640. A code check could flag every n×p form with no single-pitch dimension, but the book limits it to cases where confusion is possible.
quote: If there is any possibility of confusion between the pitch and the number of pitches, one pitch should be dimensioned.

rule: A curve made of circular arcs is dimensioned by its radii, with coordinates used only where radii are impracticable.
quote: A curved line composed of circular arcs should preferably be dimensioned by radii, and co-ordinates should only be used if the preferred is impracticable.

rule: Spacing of holes or other features on a curved part states the surface on which it is measured and whether the dimension is chordal or along the arc.
source_document: Westermann Tables for the Metal Trade (Jutz-Scharkus), revised to Indian Standards; in PARI's WP Specific Guidelines (WESTERMANN_TABLES.pdf, a scan)
source_section: Dimensioning of curved surfaces, chords, arcs, bent parts, countersinks and counterbores (pdf 72L, book 138)
note: The book spells cordal. The vision summary must say the features sit on a curved surface.
quote: care should be taken to indicate clearly on which surface the dimensioned points are to be measured and whether the dimensions are cordal or circular.

rule: Bent parts are dimensioned to the mould (construction) line where the adjoining plane surfaces meet, not to the centre of the bend arc.
note: adds detail to SM-08. Sheet metal and bent parts; out of v1 scope. Also fits MP-14.
quote: The intersection of the plane surfaces adjoining the bend is called a mould or construction line, and this line is used in dimensioning rather than the centre of the arc.

rule: A countersunk hole callout gives the hole diameter, the countersink diameter and the included angle, and the angle is 90° where the countersink seats a countersunk-head screw.
source_document: Westermann Tables for the Metal Trade (Jutz-Scharkus), revised to Indian Standards; in PARI's WP Specific Guidelines (WESTERMANN_TABLES.pdf, a scan)
source_section: Dimensioning of curved surfaces, chords, arcs, bent parts, countersinks and counterbores (pdf 72L, book 138)
supporting_reference: related rule MX-001; Westermann Tables Details of tapers, IS: 3458-1966 (pdf 52L, book 98)
note: Values come from the text layer. A missing angle also fits MX-009. Solid Edge writes hole callouts with symbol-font glyphs, so a text search finds none on the client PDFs; the check needs the decoded symbols (Spike D).
quote: The method of dimensioning a counter sunk hole. 90° ... 12ϕ ... 6ϕ

rule: A counterbored hole callout gives the hole diameter, the counterbore diameter and the counterbore depth (e.g. 6ϕ, 12ϕ, depth 6).
source_document: Westermann Tables for the Metal Trade (Jutz-Scharkus), revised to Indian Standards; in PARI's WP Specific Guidelines (WESTERMANN_TABLES.pdf, a scan)
source_section: Dimensioning of curved surfaces, chords, arcs, bent parts, countersinks and counterbores (pdf 72L, book 138)
supporting_reference: related rule MX-003
note: Solid Edge writes hole callouts with symbol-font glyphs, so a text search finds none on the client PDFs; the check needs the decoded symbols (Spike D).
quote: The method of dimensioning a counter bored hole. 12ϕ ... 6ϕ ... 6

rule: Where needed, a thread's length of full thread, or the distance to the end of full thread, is dimensioned.
note: adds detail to MX-004. The figure labels 25 Maximum length (full thread) and 35 Minimum length (including runout); a check could also confirm the length with run-out is not shorter than the full-thread length. Where necessary makes a missing length a warning unless the thread meets a shoulder (MC-003).
quote: The length of full thread or the distance to the end of full thread should be specified where necessary, as shown here.

rule: A left-hand thread is marked LH in its callout, since unmarked threads are taken as right-hand, and on a part with both hands each thread states its hand (e.g. M6 LH, M6 RH).
note: adds detail to MX-004. The figure writes L.H. and R.H. with full stops; accept both. A missing LH cannot be detected from text alone; the code check covers the format and parts that carry both hands. Each thread stating its hand comes from the figure.
quote: All threads on bolts, nuts and screws are assumed to be right-hand, unless otherwise stated ... it should be clearly indicated by the abbreviation 'LH'.

rule: A blind drilled hole is drawn ending in a 120° drill-point cone.
note: Representation only; many CAD libraries use 118°. The book says nothing about how blind-hole depth is measured.
quote: Drilled hole ... 120°

rule: In a blind threaded hole the drilled depth exceeds the threaded depth, and both depths are dimensioned.
note: same rule as MC-004. From the figures; the book gives no numeric allowance (MC-004 uses about 3 pitches).
quote: Tapped hole ... Stud in threaded hole ... Drilled hole ... Threaded hole ... Thread on stud

rule: Each structural member is called out with its number, section and size, and cut length (e.g. 2L 80×80×6.0, 7315 long).
note: adds detail to WF-10. Structural steelwork. PARI welded fabrications built from profiles could use the same check if brought into scope.
quote: 2L 80x80x6.0, 7315 long ... 2L 60×60×6.0, 3658 long ... Example of dimensioning for structural steel work (all dimensions in mm)

rule: Every plate in a fabrication has its thickness stated (e.g. 10 mm gusset plate).
note: same rule as MX-015.
quote: 10mm gusset plate

rule: The general tolerance note names IS 2102 and one of its classes: fine, medium, coarse or extra coarse.
note: adds detail to TB-008. Book edition is IS 2102-1969. PARI uses separate machining and fabrication tables; the book does not say which class each uses, so confirm the mapping with PARI before checking values.
quote: Allowable deviations for dimensions without specified tolerances IS: 2102-1969 ... Class of deviation ... Fine ... Medium ... Coarse ... Extra coarse

rule: A general-tolerance table printed on the drawing (linear or angular) matches IS 2102 for the class it names.
source_document: Westermann Tables for the Metal Trade (Jutz-Scharkus), revised to Indian Standards; in PARI's WP Specific Guidelines (WESTERMANN_TABLES.pdf, a scan)
source_section: Allowable deviations for dimensions without specified tolerances, IS 2102-1969 (pdf 73L, book 140)
supporting_reference: related rule TB-008; Westermann Tables Allowable deviations for dimensions without specified tolerances, IS 2102-1969 (pdf 73L, book 140)
note: PARI's template table follows this book's IS 2102-1969: the 'UNSPECIFIED TOL.(M)' linear and angular tables on a PARI sample drawing equal its medium row, with steps at 120-315 and 315-1000 mm (ISO 2768-1 steps at 400 mm instead). So the IS 2102 lookup table should be built from this edition (pdf 73L). Fine has no values above 4000 mm, and coarse and extra coarse none up to 3 mm.
quote: Deviations for linear dimensions ... Class of deviation ... Above ... Upto and including ... Fine ... Medium ... Coarse ... Extra coarse

rule: Untoleranced angles take the IS 2102-1969 angular deviation for their class and for the length of the shorter side of the angle, and any angular table on the drawing matches it.
note: Each deviation is given in angle units (Δα) and in mm (Δm). Fine and medium share one row. The shorter-side length needs the geometry of the two legs of the angle.
quote: Deviations for angular dimensions ... Length (L) of shorter side of angle in mm ... Fine and medium ... Coarse ... Extra coarse

rule: A rolled steel or aluminium section called out by IS designation uses a listed prefix with that section's size format (e.g. ISRO 20, 10 ISF 3, ISST 100×2.5, ISA 30 20, ISMC 125, ISALC 40×20×2).
note: adds detail to MF-003. Only checks callouts that use these codes; PARI stock callouts may use other forms, so whether to require them is a PARI question. The angle examples (ISA 20 20) omit thickness, unlike 2L 80×80×6.0 on pdf 73L.
quote: ISRO 20 Round bar, hot rolled steel, 20 mm ... 10 ISF 3 Steel flat, hot rolled, 10 mm width, 3 mm thickness

rule: Rivets on structural drawings use the IS 696-1960 symbols for shop and site rivets, snap-headed or countersunk on the near, far or both sides, and for open holes.
note: Riveted structures.
quote: Shop snap headed rivets ... Shop CSK (near side) rivets ... Site CSK (far side) rivets ... Open hole

rule: Springs are drawn in the conventional or schematic representation for compression and tension springs.
note: Springs are bought-out items or have their own drawings.
quote: Springs 1.Compression spring used with bolt and nut ... 3.Compression spring, schematic notation ... 5.Tension spring, schematic notation

rule: Gears are drawn in the conventional representation shown for spur, bevel and worm gears, alone and in mesh.
note: Gear data itself is MX-018. Gears may appear among round parts.
quote: Spur gear ... Alternative ... Spur gears (assembly) ... Bevel gear ... Worm wheel ... Worm wheel (assembly)

rule: Weld symbols on the drawing are from the IS 696-1960 set for each form of weld (fillet, square, V, U, bevel and J butts, stud, seal, spot, seam, plug, backing strip and others).
note: adds detail to WF-01. Some symbols may differ from the ISO 2553 or AWS symbols PARI uses; the PARI welding standard (WF-007) decides. Vision cannot read symbols; needs the symbol font or vector shapes.
quote: Form of weld ... Sectional representation ... Appropriate symbol ... Fillet ... Square butt ... Single V butt ... Double V butt

rule: Each weld symbol states the type, size and position of the weld.
note: same rule as WF-01. Heading of the IS 696-1960 welding table.
quote: Type size and position of welds in fusion-welded joints using the gas or arc welding process

rule: The weld arrow is placed immediately next to the joint it refers to, positioned for clarity.
quote: The position of the arrow is chosen for purposes of clarity. Normally it would be placed immediately adjacent to the joint.

rule: A fillet weld symbol carries the weld size s in front of the symbol, and an unequal-leg fillet weld gives both leg sizes (e.g. 10×6).
note: adds detail to WF-01. The figure shows s as the leg length; ISO 2553 distinguishes throat (a) and leg (z) prefixes, so the PARI convention decides how to read the number. Text next to the symbol should be in the text layer.
quote: Size of fillet weld ... sV ... Size of unequal welds ... 10×6

rule: An intermittent fillet weld gives its weld length and spacing as length(spacing), e.g. 50(100), with a leading (gap) when it starts with an unwelded length, e.g. (100)50(100), and staggered welds are given on each side.
note: adds detail to MX-026. Whether the bracketed 100 is the pitch or the gap is not clear from the figure [?]. Old IS notation; ISO 2553 writes n × l (e). MX-026 (v1) already requires length and pitch; this adds the format.
quote: Regular intermittent fillet welds commencing with a weld ... 50(100) ... commencing with an unwelded length ... (100)50(100) ... Staggered intermittent fillet welds

rule: Each material is named by a standard grade designation (e.g. St 42-W, C 45, 40 Cr 1, CuZn40, an IS aluminium grade), not by a generic name such as 'M.S.', 'STEEL', 'BRASS' or 'ALUMINIUM' alone.
note: same rule as MF-01. Same as MF-01; the book is a published source for it. PARI drawings write 'M.S.' widely (and '#' = see parts list on 86% of sheets, which must be resolved to the parts-list entry), so this fires often until PARI says whether 'M.S.' is acceptable. PARI may or may not still use the IS 1762 designation style.
quote: Symbolic Designation of essential properties of materials (iron and steel) Examples and Explanations ... St 32—0 ... C 30 ... CS 125 ... FG 15

rule: A steel named by tensile strength uses the IS form 'St' + minimum tensile strength in kgf/mm² + quality letters (e.g. St 42-W, St 55-HTW), and the combination is one the IS structural steel tables list.
note: adds detail to MF-01. Old convention: the number is kgf/mm² (St 42 is roughly 410 N/mm²). PARI may or may not still use it; the book does not say what replaced it. Letter meanings are on pdf 07R (book 9).
quote: 1. Letter St 2. Minimum tensile strength in kgf/mm² ... e.g. St. 42 Steel having a minimum tensile strength of 42 kgf/mm²

rule: A plain carbon steel named in the carbon-content system is written C + its average carbon content in hundredths of a percent (C 45 = 0.45 % C), with a manganese index only where the grade has one (C 35 Mn 75, C 55 Mn 75) and an optional K for special S and P limits.
note: adds detail to MF-01. PARI's 'C-45' fits this style with a hyphen, so the check must accept C45, C 45 and C-45. Treatment suffixes (C 45q) are handled by WST-107 and WST-108.
quote: Letter C for carbon ... Index number for carbon following letter C, denoting average Carbon content in hundredths of a percent ... e.g. C 35

rule: An alloy steel designation gives the carbon index (hundredths of a percent; prefixed T for alloy tool steels) followed by the symbols of the significant alloying elements in descending order of content, each with its alloy index (below 1 %: hundredths, underlined; 1 % and over: rounded to a whole number), e.g. 15 Cr 65, 20 Cr 18 Ni 2, 40 Ni 2 Cr 1 Mo 28.
note: adds detail to MF-01. The underline marking a below-1 % index may not survive in the PDF text layer, so ordering by content must infer it (Cr 65 = 0.65 %, Ni 2 = 2 %). PARI also writes EN numbers (EN9, EN24 in WPM-005); PARI may or may not use this IS style.
quote: Chemical symbols of the significant elements arranged in descending order of percentage contents ... Alloy Index indicating the average percentage of each alloying element

rule: A steel designation written in the IS system names a grade that exists in the IS grade tables (e.g. C 45, 40 Cr 1, 15 Cr 65, 40 Ni 2 Cr 1 Mo 28, T 105 Cr 1 Mn 60); a near-miss such as 'C 54' or '40 Cr 2' is flagged.
note: adds detail to MF-011. Grade lists are 1960s-70s editions. PARI's EN names (EN9, EN24) and later IS names must pass through or be mapped, so a miss should raise a query until PARI's material list (MF-011) exists.

rule: When a material callout cites an IS standard with the grade, the grade belongs to that standard (e.g. St 42-W to IS 2062, C 10 or 15 Cr 65 to IS 4432, C 45 to IS 5517, IS 3930 or IS 2073).
note: adds detail to MF-01. The book's grade-to-standard map is from 1960s-70s editions and several standards have been revised since (the book does not say how), so PARI needs to supply a current map. PARI may or may not cite IS numbers with grades.
quote: IS No. ... 2062 ... St 42—W ... 5517 Heat-treatable steels ... C 30 ... 4432 Case-hardening steels ... C 10c

rule: A treatment or condition letter appended to a steel designation is one of the IS symbols: a annealed or softened, c case carburized, d hard drawn or cold reduced, h hot-rolled, n normalized, o spheroidized, p patented, q hardened and tempered, s stress relieved, t tempered (quality letters A, E, L, D, D1, R, G, H, I, M; K for special S and P limits).
note: adds detail to MF-01. E and R each mean both a steel quality and a steelmaking process in the book, so a parser needs position rules. PARI drawings seen state heat treatment as a note, not a suffix; PARI may or may not use these letters.
quote: Treatment given a–Annealed or softened c–Case carburized d–Hard drawn, cold reduced h–Hot-rolled n–Normalized o–Spherodized p–Patented q–Hardened and tempered s–Stress relieved t–Tempered

rule: A treatment letter in the material designation (e.g. C 45q hardened and tempered, 15 Cr 3c case carburized, T 50a annealed) agrees with the heat-treatment field and notes; e.g. an 'a' (annealed) designation with a note asking for hardening is flagged.
note: adds detail to NM-002. Fires only when a suffix is present; PARI drawings seen don't use suffixes, so expect few hits. Example 15 Cr 3c is on pdf 05L (book 4).
quote: T 50a T —Tool steel; a=annealed ... C 45q q —Hardened and tempered

rule: A casting material is named by its IS casting designation and grade, the number being the minimum tensile strength in kgf/mm²: FG grey iron (FG 15-40), SG spheroidal graphite iron (e.g. SG 80/2), BM, PM and WM malleable iron, CS steel castings (CS 41-125), and the special prefixes CSH, CSC, AFG, ASG, ABR.
note: adds detail to MF-01. Castings are out of v1 scope. Grades are in kgf/mm²; PARI may or may not still use these. Grade tables are on pdf 05L (book 4). 'Tensile strengths are on 30 mm Dia Test Bars as-cast.'
quote: FG 15—Grey iron castings with minimum tensile strength 15 kgf/mm² ... BM 35—Black heart malleable iron castings with minimum tensile strength 35 kgf/mm²

rule: A copper alloy is designated Cu followed by the other significant elements in decreasing order of content (alphabetical when equal), each with its index (1 % and over rounded to a whole number), e.g. CuZn40, CuSn8Zn4, CuZn42Pb2; a cast alloy carries a prefix G (sand), GK (chill), GD (die) or GZ (continuous), and no prefix means wrought.
note: adds detail to MF-01. PARI may write 'BRASS', 'PHOSPHOR BRONZE' or a grade such as IS 318 Grade II (pdf 10L, book 14) instead; PARI may or may not use this style. A G/GK/GD/GZ prefix means a cast blank.
quote: Other significant elements follow in the order of decreasing percentage or when equal in alphabetical order ... Absence of these symbols indicate that the material is in wrought form.

rule: A pure-copper part names its IS 191 grade (ETP, FRHC, FRTP-1, FRTP-2, ATP or OF), and a conductor uses a high-conductivity grade (FRHC or OF; ETP for electrical parts).
note: adds detail to MF-007. Electrical parts are out of v1 scope; listed for completeness.
quote: Electrolytic tough pitch copper ETP 99.9% Cu Soft For electrical parts ... Oxygen free high conductivity copper OF 99.95% Cu High conductivity For conductors

rule: An aluminium alloy named in the IS 6051 numeric system has five digits for a wrought alloy or four for a casting alloy, with a first digit from 1 to 8 naming the major alloying group (1 unalloyed, 2 Cu, 3 Mn, 4 Si, 5 Mg, 6 Mg2Si, 7 Zn, 8 other; 9 unassigned).
note: adds detail to MF-01. Conflict: a four-digit Aluminium Association wrought number such as 6061 or 6082 reads as an IS 6051 casting designation, so the drawing should say which system it uses. PARI's aluminium naming is unknown; PARI may or may not use IS 6051.
quote: Wrought aluminium alloys (five digit system) First digit Identifies the major alloying element ... Casting alloys (four digit system)

rule: A heat-treatable aluminium alloy is called out with its condition (e.g. IS 734 HF grades in the fully heat treated condition, IS 617 casting suffix M, W or WP), because the book gives different minimum strengths by condition (A-11-W 22.0 and A-11-WP 28.3 kgf/mm² sand cast).
note: adds detail to MF-01. The book doesn't define the M, W, WP suffixes on these pages; the A-11-W / A-11-WP values are on pdf 10R (book 15). Modern drawings use temper codes (e.g. -T6), which the book doesn't cover; PARI may or may not use these IS designations.
quote: Tensile strength in “O” condition, kgf/mm², min. ... (Fully heat treated condition) ... HF 15 Combines high strength with fair ductility in the solution treated condition

rule: A part machined from phenolic laminate or moulding material names its type and grade (IS 2038 fabric laminate F1-F3, IS 2036 paper laminate P1-P5, IS 1300 phenolic moulding grade 1-8), and the grade suits the use: F1 fine machining, F2 small gears, F3 high impact, P3-P5 electrical insulation.
note: adds detail to MF-007. Trade names such as 'Bakelite' or 'Formica' (the book's own examples, pdf 11R, book 17) don't give the grade. PARI's use of laminates is unknown; warning only.
quote: F 1 ... Made from fine-weave cotton fabric, for components requiring fine machining ... F 3 ... For components requiring high impact strength

rule: On a welded fabrication, steel members named by IS structural grade use a weldable quality (St 42-W or St 55-HTW; St 42-S only 'upon certain conditions'), not St 58-HT, which is meant for structures not fabricated by welding, nor the ordinary St 32-O / St 42-O.
note: adds detail to MF-007. Old designations; PARI fabrication drawings write 'M.S.', which says nothing about weld quality. PARI may or may not still use these grades.
quote: St 42-W ... Can be subjected to fusion welding. St 58-HT ... Intended for use in structures where fabrication is done by methods other than welding.

rule: Through hardening, flame hardening or induction hardening is not specified on a steel standardized only by tensile strength (St grades, structural steel, 'M.S.'); the IS system puts those grades in the group of steels not required to receive heat treatment.
note: adds detail to WPM-001. Treating 'M.S.' as a tensile-strength grade is an assumption. Case carburizing of low-carbon steel is handled by WST-119; PARI's own table (WPM-001) decides what PARI allows.
quote: Steels not required to receive heat treatment ... Applicable for steels which are standardized on the basis of their tensile strength without detailed chemical composition

rule: Flame or induction hardening is specified only on a steel suited to it, such as those IS 3930 lists: C 30, C 45, T 70, 37 Mn 2, 40 Mn 2 S 12, 35 Mn 2 Mo 45, 50 Cr 1, 50 Cr 1 V 23, 40 Ni 3, 40 Ni 2 Cr 1 Mo 28, 31 Ni 3 Cr 65 Mo 55.
note: adds detail to WPM-001. 1966 list; PARI's table (WPM-001) governs. EN names (e.g. EN8, EN9, EN24) need mapping, which the book doesn't give.
quote: These wrought unalloyed and alloyed steels for flame and induction hardening are used when high core strength and good impact properties are required.

rule: The surface hardness specified for a flame- or induction-hardened steel does not exceed the hardness IS 3930 gives as obtainable for that grade (e.g. C 30 45-50 HRC, C 45 55-61 HRC, 50 Cr 1 57-62 HRC, 40 Ni 2 Cr 1 Mo 28 54-60 HRC).
note: adds detail to WPM-002. Catches e.g. 'C-45 INDUCTION HARDEN 58-62 HRC' (62 > 61). A spec below the range is achievable and is not flagged. HV or HB specs convert through the hardness table.
quote: Surface hardness obtainable HRC ... C 30 45–50 C 45 55–61 T 70 60–63

rule: Case hardening (carburizing) is specified on a steel IS 4432 lists as a case-hardening steel (C 10, C 14, 15 Cr 65, 17 Mn 1 Cr 95, 20 Mn Cr 1, 16 Ni Cr 2 Mo 20 and the others) or on a free-cutting grade marked suitable for it (10 S 11, 14 Mn 1 S 14); other materials are queried.
note: adds detail to WPM-001. The book lists C 45 under flame/induction and hardening-and-tempering, not case hardening. Case carburizing 'M.S.' is common shop practice but isn't listed; PARI's table (WPM-001) decides. Third entry of the first grade row is unclear ('19S11' [?]). Free-cutting note 'Suitable also for case hardening' is on pdf 07L (book 8).
quote: These steels are used for components requiring high wear resistant surfaces, coupled with tough cores to resist shock loads and strength to give longer service life.

rule: Hardening and tempering (through hardening) is specified on a steel IS 5517 lists for the hardened and tempered condition (e.g. C 30 to C 55 Mn 75, 40 Cr 1, 40 Cr 1 Mo 28, 40 Ni 2 Cr 1 Mo 28) or on a tool steel (IS 3748 / IS 3749 T-grades); other materials are queried.
note: adds detail to WPM-001. Tool steels are 'capable of being hardened and tempered' (pdf 08L, book 10). PARI's table (WPM-001) governs; EN names need mapping.
quote: These wrought unalloyed and alloyed steels in the form of billets and bars for general engineering purposes are intended to be used in the hardened and tempered condition.

rule: A tensile strength, or a hardness converted to tensile strength, specified for a hardened-and-tempered part does not exceed the range IS 5517 gives for that grade in that condition (e.g. C 45 60-75, C 50 80-95, 40 Cr 1 80-95, 40 Ni 2 Cr 1 Mo 28 120-135 kgf/mm²); a higher value is queried.
note: adds detail to WPM-002. Warning only: IS 5517 ranges apply at its tempering temperatures (about 500-720 °C), and a drawing may deliberately call a harder, low-temper condition. C 45 at 60-75 kgf/mm² is about 175-220 HV on the comparison table, below the HRC range, so 'C 45 H&T 40-45 HRC' would be queried; this may conflict with PARI practice.
quote: Properties in hardened and tempered condition Tensile strength kgf/mm² ... C 45 60 to 75 ... Tempering temperature °C ... 530 to 670

rule: A part made from a case-hardening steel (IS 4432) or a tool steel (IS 3748 / IS 3749) states its heat treatment and hardness, or states that none is required, since the book lists these grades for hardened use and gives tool steels' hardness only as an annealed maximum.
note: adds detail to MF-005. Not applied to C 30-C 45, which IS 2073 also lists as black bars for machined parts with no heat treatment (pdf 07L, book 8).
quote: ...for cold work, capable of being hardened and tempered. These are used for the making tools and dies for blanking, trimming, shaping and shearing.

rule: A heat-treatment requirement is applied only to a metal part; a part in a plastic or laminate (thermoplastics soften at about 60-120 °C) carries no heat treatment.

source_section: Heat treatment of iron and steel-glossary of terms, IS: 1956-1962; Engineering Plastics (pdf 65R, book 125)

note: Softening range is from pdf 11R (book 17): 'Thermoplastics soften at high temperature, normally between 60°C and 120°C.' Catches heat-treatment notes copied from a steel drawing (NM-008). Book page of pdf 65R inferred.
quote: Heat treatment: Combination of heating and cooling operation in a prescribed manner ... to induce desired properties in metals and alloys in the solid state.

rule: A heat-treatment note names a specific process in IS 1956 terms (e.g. normalizing, full annealing, hardening and tempering, case hardening or carburizing, flame hardening, induction hardening, nitriding, stress relieving, sub-zero treatment, spheroidizing), not a generic 'HEAT TREAT' or a bare 'HARDEN' that leaves the process open.
note: adds detail to MF-005. IS 1956 'hardening' covers quenching and cold working alike, so 'HARDEN' alone doesn't say which. 'HARDEN 58-62 HRC' does state the result, which NM-12 prefers; PARI to say whether that is enough. Book page inferred.
quote: Hardening: Any process which increases the hardness, for example, quenching from or above the transformation range, or cold working.

rule: 'Case hardening' is used only for hardening by changing the surface composition (carburizing, nitriding); a surface hardened by heating and quenching without a composition change is flame or induction hardening, so 'CASE HARDEN' on a flame/induction grade such as C 45 is queried.
note: adds detail to WPM-001. Shop shorthand often writes 'case hardening' with a case depth for induction-hardened C 45, which leaves the shop two processes to choose from. May conflict with PARI notes such as 'CASE DEPTH 0.8~1.2 MM'. Book page inferred.
quote: Case hardening: Hardening the surface by changing its composition followed by, if necessary, suitable heat treatment. ... Flame hardening: Rapid heating of the surface by means of an oxy-gas flame

rule: Treatments defined only for hardened steel (tempering, sub-zero treatment) appear together with a hardening process on the same part; a 'TEMPER' or 'SUB-ZERO' note with no hardening is flagged.

note: Fires on 3 client PDFs, all with the note 'TO BE TEMPERING UPTO 52~55 HRC' and a case depth but no hardening process named, which leaves the shop to guess the process. Book page inferred.
quote: Sub-zero treatment: Treatment given to certain hardened steels by cooling to temperatures below zero (0°C) ... Tempering: Heating ... below transformation zone of hardened steels

rule: When the only heat treatment named is a softening one (annealing, spheroidizing, sub-critical annealing, stress relieving), the drawing does not also ask for a hardened-level hardness (e.g. 'ANNEALED, 58-62 HRC'); the book lists annealed tool steels at 200-260 HB max.

note: Annealed maxima are from pdf 08L (book 10). Stress relieving after hardening is normal, so the rule fires only when no hardening process is named. Book page inferred.
quote: Stress relieving (stabilizing): Heating to and if necessary, holding at a sufficiently high temperature below the transformation range followed by slow cooling to remove internal stresses only.

rule: A hardness requirement states its scale with the value: Vickers HV, Brinell HB, Rockwell HRC (C scale, 150 kgf) or HRB (B scale, 100 kgf).
note: same rule as MF-010. Same as MF-010 (minus the case-depth part); the book is a published source for it. IS number only partly legible; book page inferred.
quote: Vickers Hardness Number, HV ... Brinell Hardness Number, HB ... Rockwell Hardness Number, HR ... C Scale 150 kgf Load ... B Scale 100 kgf Load

rule: A hardness value lies in the working range of its scale (HRC 20-67, HRB 60-99, HB up to 400 with a steel ball or 700 with a carbide ball); a value outside it (e.g. '15 HRC', '450 HB', '250 HRC') means the wrong scale or a typo.

note: Values below 20 HRC belong in HB or HRB. Read '58 ± 2 HRC' as 56-60. No client drawing fires; the only hits are in PARI's guideline PDFs. IS number only partly legible; book page inferred.
quote: limited to materials having a maximum Brinell Hardness of 400 with steel ball and of 700 with carbide ball ... HRc between 20 to 67 ... HRb between 60 to 99

rule: Where a hardness is given in two scales, or together with a tensile strength (e.g. '58-62 HRC (650-750 HV)'), the values agree with the IS hardness comparison table for steel.
source_document: Westermann Tables for the Metal Trade (Jutz-Scharkus), revised to Indian Standards; in PARI's WP Specific Guidelines (WESTERMANN_TABLES.pdf, a scan)
source_section: Hardness Comparison Tables For Steel, IS: [?]58-1967 (pdf 66R, book 127)
note: The tolerance is an assumption; table steps are 15-40 HV. Steel only. IS number only partly legible; book page inferred.
quote: Hardness Comparison Tables For Steel ... 700 ... 656 60.1 ... 660 ... 620 58.3

rule: Hardness of a nitrided or thin case-hardened surface is specified in Vickers (HV), the scale the hardness table names as suited to very hard, very thin, case-hardened and nitrided material.
note: adds detail to MF-010. PARI drawings state hardness in HRC; whether PARI wants HV for nitrided or QPQ parts is open. The book says HV is suited, not that other scales are wrong. Book page inferred.
quote: Can be applied on all materials. Suited specially for testing very hard and very thin materials and also case-hardened and nitrided steels.

rule: A stated part mass is no more than the mass of the part's bounding envelope (length × width × height, or π/4·D²·L for a round part) at the material's specific weight (e.g. steel 7.85, grey cast iron 7.2, brass 8.5, Al alloy 2.8 gf/cm³).

supporting_reference: related rule TB-014
note: Upper bound only, from the overall dimensions: a mass above it means the mass or the material is wrong (e.g. a mass left over from an aluminium version). A tight check needs the model volume (phase2_3d). Element values (Cu 8.9, Al 2.7) are on pdf 03R (book 1).
quote: Specific weight = Weight per unit volume (gf/cm³ or kgf/dm³) ... Steel 7.85 ... Gray cast iron 7.2 ... Brass 8.5 ... Al-alloy (Al, Cu, Mg) 2.8

rule: Where a drawing states the bar stock for a part (e.g. 'Ø40 BAR', 'ISRO 40', 'HEX 24 A/F'), the size is a standard hot-rolled size: rounds 5, 6, 8, 10, 12, 14, 16, 18, 20, 22, 25, 28, 32, 36, 40, 45, 50, 56, 63, 71, 80, 90 or 100 mm; squares 5-100 mm; hexagons 5-60 mm across flats.
note: adds detail to MF-003. The series omits sizes such as 30 and 35 mm, so PARI's stock list should decide; PARI may or may not use ISRO/ISSQ. Column headers print 'IS: 1723-1971' and 'IS: 1732-1971'; pdf 05R (book 5) gives IS 1732 for round and square bars. Non-ferrous bar sizes are on pdf 15R (book 25).
quote: Examples for standard designation: ISRO 20 : Round bar of 20 mm Ø ISSQ 20 : Square bar of side width 20 mm

rule: A steel flat is called out by width and thickness in mm (IS form: width, ISF, thickness, e.g. 10 ISF 3), and the width × thickness pair is one the IS 1731 table lists (widths 10-300 mm, thicknesses 4-60 mm).
note: adds detail to MF-003. Old 'ISF' form; PARI's stock callout style is unknown and PARI may or may not use it. Steel strip (IS: 1730-1961, 'ISST 100×2.5') is on the same page and is sheet-metal stock.
quote: Hot rolled steel flats confirming to this standard, shall be designated by their width in mm., followed by letters ISF and the thickness in mm.

rule: A rolled or extruded section on a fabrication drawing is called out by its IS designation (ISA, ISNT, ISDT, ISLT, ISMT, ISJC, ISLC, ISMC, ISCG, ISJB, ISLB, ISMB, ISWB, ISHB; aluminium ISALT, ISALA, ISALB, ISALC), and that size exists in the IS section tables.
note: adds detail to MF-003. Tables are 1964-71 editions; a size missing from them may exist in a later edition, so a miss is a query. Tee bars and channels are on pdf 14L (book 22), angles on pdf 13R (book 21), aluminium sections on pdf 16L (book 26).
quote: Classification: (a) Indian Standard Junior Beams–ISJB (b) Indian Standard Light Weight Beams–ISLB (c) Indian Standard Medium Weight Beams–ISMB

rule: An angle section callout gives both leg lengths and the thickness (e.g. ISA 50×50×6), because IS 808 lists several thicknesses for each leg size (ISA 50×50 in 3, 4, 5 and 6 mm).
note: adds detail to MX-015. The book's own example 'ISA 2020' omits thickness; the rule follows from the table listing several thicknesses per size. PARI's angle callout style is unknown.
quote: Indian standard equal angle of size A=20 mm and B=20 mm may be designated as ISA 2020.

rule: Where the IS 808 table lists more than one section under one designation (ISHB 150, 200, 225, 250, 300, 350, 400, 450 and ISWB 600 come in two or three weights), the callout adds the weight per metre; provisional sizes carry their (P) mark (e.g. ISMB(P) 100).
note: adds detail to MF-003. ISMB 100 and ISMB(P)100 differ only by the (P) mark; ISLB has (P) variants too.
quote: (f) Provisional Sizes—(P) ... ISHB 150 ... 27.1 ... ISHB 150 ... 30.6 ... ISHB 150 ... 34.6

rule: A steel tube is called out by nominal bore with its class (light, medium or heavy) or by outside diameter × wall thickness, since IS 1161 gives three wall thicknesses for each nominal bore (e.g. 25 NB, 33.7 OD: 2.65, 3.25 or 4.05 mm), and the combination exists in the table.
note: adds detail to MX-015. Aluminium, brass and copper tube OD × wall tables (IS: 2678-1972, IS: 407-1966, IS: 5493-1969) are on the same page.

rule: When a stock or section callout cites an IS standard, the standard matches the product form: IS 808 beams, channels and angles; IS 1173 tee bars; IS 1730 plates, sheet and strip; IS 1731 flats; IS 1732 round and square bars; IS 1864 unequal angles; IS 3954 channels for general engineering; IS 1161 steel tubes.
note: adds detail to NM-03. IS 1161 (tubes) is from pdf 16R (book 27). The list gives IS 1864 for unequal angles but pdf 13R (book 21) shows unequal angles under IS 808-1964, so both should pass. Fires only when an IS number is cited.
quote: 808 Beam, channel and angle sections ... 1731 Flats ... 1732 Round and square bars ... 1864 Unequal angles

rule: A brazing or soldering note names the filler alloy by its IS designation (IS 2927 BA-AlSi, BA-CuZn, BA-CuAg; IS 193 Sn grades), and the filler suits the base metals: BA-AlSi for aluminium and its alloys, BA-CuAg 12 for carbide tips to shanks and stainless steels, BA-CuZn 8 for steels and nickel alloys.
note: No brazing or soldering note on any of the 1,175 client PDFs; encode it only if PARI brazes. Brazing hasn't been seen on PARI samples; fires only when a brazing or soldering note exists.
quote: BA-AlSi 1 ... General purpose brazing alloy for torch, dip and furnace brazing of aluminium and its alloys ... BA-CuAg 12 ... For brazing carbide tips to shanks, and stainless steels.

rule: A sheet or strip part names its IS grade (IS 513 / IS 1079 types O, D, DD, EDD; IS 4030 temper No. 1-5) and, if electroplated, the fine or bright surface finish meant for electroplating, not the medium or dull finish marked not suitable for plating.
note: adds detail to WPS-003. Sheet metal is out of v1 scope. IS 4030 strip finishes are on pdf 07L (book 8).
quote: Medium or dull for general purposes (not suitable for plating) Fine or bright for electroplating

rule: Stock sizes stated for wrought material (bar diameter, plate or flat thickness) are preferred nominal sizes from IS 1136, favouring sizes derived from R10 over R20 and then the remaining sizes.
note: adds detail to MF-003. PARI's own stock list, if it has one, should override this table; warning only. The R10 > R20 > rest order is from the 'Selection of a single size' paragraph.
quote: Preferred nominal sizes in millimeters ... For wrought metal products ... Numbers indicated in bold type are the preferred ones.

rule: The basic size of a feature toleranced by a fit symbol is a whole number, preferably a preferred size from IS 1136.
note: Preferred basic sizes are advice for the designer; many functional sizes are legitimately not preferred numbers. The preferred-size part comes from the IS 1136 'Selection of a single size' text (pdf 41L). Info only: many functional sizes are legitimately not preferred numbers.
quote: For the sake of convenience, a basic size, which is usually a whole number (e.g., 20, 75, etc.) is given to represent the dimension of a part.

rule: Where a dimension shows both its deviations and its limits of size, each limit equals the basic size plus the matching deviation, and the tolerance equals upper minus lower deviation.
source_document: Westermann Tables for the Metal Trade (Jutz-Scharkus), revised to Indian Standards; in PARI's WP Specific Guidelines (WESTERMANN_TABLES.pdf, a scan)
source_section: Limits and Fits, Terminology for ISO System, IS: 919-1963 (pdf 41R, book 77)
note: Book example: 20 -0.045/-0.195 gives limits 19.955 and 19.805, tolerance 0.150. Also covers a fit symbol shown with limit sizes in brackets.
quote: Upper deviation: The algebraic difference between the maximum limit and the corresponding basic size.

rule: In a dimension with two deviations, the upper deviation is algebraically larger than the lower one and is written above it.
note: same rule as RQ-002. The book's example writes -0.045 above -0.195. The 'written above' part needs text positions from the text layer.
quote: The difference between the maximum and minimum limits of sizes is the tolerance. It is also equal to the algebraic difference between the upper and lower deviations.

rule: A fit symbol uses a valid tolerance-position letter (a to zc without i, l, o, q and w, plus js; capitals for holes) followed by a grade from 01, 0 and 1 to 16.
note: adds detail to TL-013. Grades from pdf 42L ('0, 01, 1, ..., 16 ... in all 18 grades'). The 25-letter list is the book's; if PARI drawings use other letter combinations, confirm before treating them as errors.
quote: The letters a...js, j...z, za, zb, zc (letters i, l, o, q, w are omitted) determine the position of tolerance zone with reference to zero line (in all 25 positions).

rule: A fit symbol on an internal feature (hole, bore, slot) uses a capital letter (e.g. H7) and one on an external feature (shaft, pin, tongue) a lower-case letter (e.g. g6).
source_document: Westermann Tables for the Metal Trade (Jutz-Scharkus), revised to Indian Standards; in PARI's WP Specific Guidelines (WESTERMANN_TABLES.pdf, a scan)
source_section: Limits and Fits, IS Symbols, IS: 919-1963 (pdf 42L, book 78)
supporting_reference: related rule TL-013
note: Needs the vision summary to say whether the dimension is on an internal or external feature, and the text layer to keep letter case.
quote: Holes: capital letters (e.g. H, G, M) are used to designate the position of tolerance zone. ... Shafts: small letters (e.g. h, g, m) are used

rule: Where a fit symbol is given with numeric deviations or limits, they match the IS 919 deviation table for that tolerance zone and size range (e.g. Ø20 H7 = +0.021/0).
source_document: Westermann Tables for the Metal Trade (Jutz-Scharkus), revised to Indian Standards; in PARI's WP Specific Guidelines (WESTERMANN_TABLES.pdf, a scan)
source_section: Limits and Fits, IS Symbols, IS: 919-1963 (pdf 42L, book 78)
note: Tables on pdf 43L-44R (book 80-83): hole basis H6, H7, H8, H11 and shaft basis h5 to h11, 0-500 mm, in µm. Zones not in the tables get no finding. Second worked example on the page: 20 d9 = -0.065/-0.117.
quote: instead of writing 20ϕ +0.021/+0, it is mentioned as 20ϕH7. The actual values of deviations corresponding to the size so mentioned can be read from tables (see pages 80-83).

rule: Tolerance grades on machined fits are in the machine-building range 5 to 11; grades 01 to 4 belong to gauges and 12 to 16 to rolled or cast surfaces.
note: adds detail to TL-003. Raise a grade finer than 5 on a machined part as major (gauge-class accuracy); a grade 12-16 on a fit as info.
quote: Grade 0, 01, 1-4 finer gr. ... 5-11 fine to coarse gr. ... 12-16 coarse gr. Application Gauge ... Machine building ... Rolling, casting

rule: Tolerance zones used for fits come from IS 919's recommended list for machine building, preferably the first-preference zones (e.g. holes H7, G7, F8; shafts f7, g6, h6, k6, m6).
note: adds detail to TL-013. Zones outside the list are unusual rather than wrong; info only.
quote: Recommended holes for machine building industry ... Recommended shafts ... * Shows first preference Without asterisk mark: Second preference

rule: Fits use the basic-hole system (H holes with shafts of varying letters) unless the mating part suits the basic-shaft system, such as bright drawn bar, ball bearings or power-transmission parts.
note: PARI's preferred fit system isn't confirmed. A non-H hole fit (e.g. Ø20 F7) would be raised as info, asking whether a basic-shaft fit was intended.
quote: Application: Machine and engine building, locomotive construction. ... Application: Electric motors, ball bearings, power transmission, products made from bright drawn bars.

rule: A fitted size is given as its basic size followed by the fit symbol (e.g. Ø20 H7), not only as the basic size with numeric deviations.
note: PARI drawings already show fits as 'Ø8 H7'. Whether PARI adds deviations in brackets, or allows deviations alone, is PARI's choice. A code check can only suggest the symbol where the deviations exactly equal a tabulated zone.
quote: the deviations are not shown directly added to the basic size, but the toleranced size is indicated by its basic size followed by a symbol consisting of a letter

rule: The diameter symbol is written after the size (20ϕ H7), as in the book's IS 919 examples.
note: Obsolete notation: PARI writes 'Ø8 H7', symbol first (DTT-007). Conflicts with DTT-007 (Ø before the value) and with PARI's own drawings, which show 'Ø8 H7'. Probably an obsolete convention; recommend not adopting it. Listed so the conflict is on record.

rule: A bolt designation states head shape and fastener type, thread size, length, pitch (fine threads only), nut type if supplied, IS number, product grade (P, S or B) and property class, e.g. 'Hex bolt M 20×1.5×75-IS:1364-S-4.6'.
note: adds detail to BM-05. The book's labelled diagram orders it M20 × 75 × 1.5 (length before pitch) but its examples write M 20 × 1.5 × 75; a parser should accept both. Property class: first number × 10 = minimum tensile strength in kgf/mm², second number = yield/tensile ratio × 10. Parts lists only.
quote: Typical examples showing the bolt designations: Hex bolt M 16×70 NL-IS:1363 Hex bolt M 20×1.5×75-IS:1364-S-4.6

rule: A metric thread callout writes the pitch only for a fine thread (M20×1.5); a coarse thread is written by size alone (M20).
note: adds detail to MX-004. An exception to MX-004: a callout with no pitch is complete (coarse pitch implied). Writing the coarse pitch is common and harmless; PARI's convention isn't confirmed, so info only.
quote: Pitch (for fine thread only)

rule: A metric thread callout uses an ISO metric size with a standard pitch: the coarse pitch for that size (e.g. M10 = 1.5, M12 = 1.75) or a fine pitch from the table (e.g. M10×1.25, M16×1.5).
note: adds detail to MC-005. Coarse sizes M1.6-M36 on book 85 (M1 and M1.2 on book 86). The fine series is only M8×1, M10×1.25, M12×1.25, M16×1.5, M20×1.5, M24×2, M30×2, M36×3 (book 86), so a size or fine pitch outside this short list should be info, not an error. Book 86 misprints the M12×1.25 pitch as 1.24.
quote: ISO Metric screw threads IS: 4218 (Part III)—1967 ... Thread size ... Pitch P ... M10 ... 1.5 ... M12 ... 1.75

rule: A thread tolerance class, where given, is one tabulated for the size, with an upper-case class for internal threads (5H, 6H, 7H) and a lower-case class for external threads (4h, 6g, 8g).
source_document: Westermann Tables for the Metal Trade (Jutz-Scharkus), revised to Indian Standards; in PARI's WP Specific Guidelines (WESTERMANN_TABLES.pdf, a scan)
source_section: ISO Metric Screw Threads, IS: 4218 (Part VI)-1967 (pdf 46L, book 86)
note: Case mismatch (e.g. 6g on a tapped hole) is major. A class not tabulated for the size (dashes: 7H below M3, 8g below M5, 6H below M1.6) or outside the book's list is info. Needs internal/external from the vision summary or callout context.
quote: Nut threads Minor diameter D1 in mm Tolerance class 5H ... 6H ... 7H ... Bolt threads ... Tolerance class 4h ... 6g ... 8g

rule: A British Standard Whitworth thread callout uses a listed inch size with its standard threads per inch.
note: Inch thread; out of scope for PARI's metric drawings (compare HNF-005, DTT-37). The Whitworth run-out/undercut table (pdf 52R) and Whitworth drill table (pdf 55R) belong to the same family.
quote: British standard whitworth threads—BSW ... Thread size d, D inches ... Threads per inch z

rule: A trapezoidal thread is called out as 'Tr d×P' for a single start, or 'Tr d×lead (P pitch)' for a multi-start thread, with 'LH' added for a left-hand thread (e.g. Tr 40×14 (P7) LH).
note: adds detail to MX-004. Right hand is the default when LH is absent. Lead screws on PARI machines are the likely users.
quote: Designation: Examples: Tr 40×7 A single start ISO metric trapezoidal screw thread ... Tr 40×14 (P7) LH A multiple start left hand ISO metric trapezoidal screw thread

rule: A trapezoidal thread uses a nominal diameter and pitch pair from the IS 7008 table (e.g. Tr 20×4, Tr 40×7), avoiding the non-preferred diameters marked * (14, 18, 22, 26, 30, 34).
note: adds detail to MC-005. A pitch that doesn't match the table is major; a non-preferred diameter is info. Table covers 8-100 mm.
quote: d Nom ... P ... 20 15.5 4 ... 40 32.0 7 ... *Non-preferred sizes

rule: For a multi-start thread, the lead is a whole multiple of the pitch (lead ÷ pitch = number of starts, e.g. Tr 40×14 (P7) has two starts).
source_document: Westermann Tables for the Metal Trade (Jutz-Scharkus), revised to Indian Standards; in PARI's WP Specific Guidelines (WESTERMANN_TABLES.pdf, a scan)
source_section: ISO Metric Trapezoidal Screw Threads, IS: 7008-1973 (pdf 47L, book 88)
note: Pure arithmetic on the callout text. One client drawing writes 'Tr 12 x 3P' (pitch 3, single start).
quote: Tr 40×14 (P7) LH A multiple start left hand ISO metric trapezoidal screw thread of Nom. dia=40mm and lead=14mm and pitch=7mm

rule: A square thread is called out as 'SQ d×P' with its IS number, using a diameter and pitch from the IS 4694 normal series (e.g. SQ 30×6).
note: adds detail to MC-005. Table covers 22-60 mm only; sizes outside it get info.
quote: Designation: Example: SQ 30×6-IS: 4694-1968 A square thread of nominal dia. 30mm and pitch 6mm

rule: A saw-tooth (buttress) thread is called out as 'ST d×P' with its IS number, using a diameter and pitch from the IS 4696 table.
note: adds detail to MC-005. The book's own example (48 × 3) isn't in its normal-series table (48 mm has pitch 8), so a pitch outside the table should be a warning, not an error.
quote: Designation: Example— ST 48 × 3–IS: 4696 A saw tooth thread of nominal diameter 48 mm and pitch 3 mm

rule: A parallel pipe thread for fastening is designated by its size from the IS 2643 table (1/8 to 2) and, for an external thread, its tolerance class A or B (e.g. 'Ext. FP 2B', 'Int. FP 2').
note: The table labels sizes 'PF' but the examples write 'FP'. PARI may call out port threads in another notation (e.g. 'G 1/8'); PARI to confirm the notation before this is encoded. Inch trade sizes are allowed under HNF-005.
quote: Designations: (1) Ext. FP 2B—External pipe thread for fastening purposes of size 2 with class B tolerance. (2) Int. FP 2—Internal pipe thread for fastening purposes of size 2.

rule: A standard bolt, screw, nut or stud named on a drawing or parts list cites the IS number for that fastener type (e.g. hexagon socket head cap screw IS 2269, slotted cheese head screw IS 1366, hexagon socket grub screw IS 6094).
note: adds detail to BM-05. Mainly parts lists; a single-part drawing names a fastener only in a note (e.g. 'FOR M6 SHCS').
quote: Hexagon socket head cap screws IS : 2269 ... Slotted cheese head screws IS : 1366 ... Hexagon socket grub screws ... IS : 6094

rule: A blind tapped hole that takes a stud has a full-thread length of at least the stud's threaded end b1: about 1×d for type A studs and 1.5×d for type B (e.g. M10: 10 or 15 mm).
note: adds detail to MC-006. The book doesn't say which stud type suits which material; MC-006's 1.5×D in aluminium matches type B. Without knowing the hole takes a stud, use 1×d as a warning threshold.
quote: HOLE IS: 4499-1968 Threaded end b1 of the thread Stud type A Stud type B ... M10 ... 10 ... 15

rule: A blind tapped hole's drill depth S exceeds its thread length b1 by at least the IS 4499 allowance for the size (e.g. type A: M6 11 vs 6, M10 16 vs 10, M20 28 vs 20 mm).
note: adds detail to MC-004. S - b1 runs from 3 mm (M3) to 11 mm (M36), about 3 to 6 pitches, so MC-004's 'about 3 pitches' is the low end. Cross-check with the internal run-out X1 of IS 1369 (WST-245).
quote: Depth S of the threaded hole Stud type A Stud type B ... M10 ... 16 ... 21

rule: A screw designation gives the type prefix A (fully threaded) or B (partially threaded) where the standard has both, size × length, IS number, and grade and property class where they apply (e.g. 'BM10×30-IS: 1365-4.8', 'M10×60-IS: 2269-P-8.8').
note: adds detail to BM-05. Parts lists only.
quote: Slotted countersunk head screw BM10×30—IS: 1365-4.8 ... B=Type B (partially threaded) Property class 4.8

rule: A rivet is designated by head type, diameter × length and IS number (e.g. 'Pan head rivet 6×30 IS: 2155'), with a preferred diameter and a preferred length for that diameter.
note: adds detail to BM-05. Riveted assemblies are outside v1 scope.
quote: Preferred shank diameter: 1.6, 2, 2.5, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 10 mm ... Designation: Example—Pan head rivet 6 × 30 IS: 2155

rule: A hole for a taper pin is called out with the 1:50 taper and the pin's nominal size, which is the small-end diameter, chosen from the standard sizes (1.5 to 50 mm).
source_document: Westermann Tables for the Metal Trade (Jutz-Scharkus), revised to Indian Standards; in PARI's WP Specific Guidelines (WESTERMANN_TABLES.pdf, a scan)
note: The drawing should make clear that the stated diameter is the small end.
quote: Taper 1:50 ... Nominal size is the diameter of the thin end of the taper pin.

rule: A taper pin is designated by type (A or B), nominal diameter × length and IS number (e.g. 'Solid taper pin A 10×50 IS: 6688'), with a standard length inside the range for that diameter.
note: adds detail to BM-05. Parts lists. Finish N6 for type A and N7 for type B (see WST-232).
quote: Designation: Example: Solid taper pin A 10×50 IS: 6688. A solid taper pin of nominal diameter 10mm of type A and nominal length 50mm

rule: A cylindrical pin is designated by diameter with tolerance class (m6, h8 or h11) × length and IS number (e.g. 'Cylindrical pin 10h8×20 IS: 2393'), with a standard length inside the range for that diameter.
note: adds detail to BM-05. Parts lists; on a part drawing the pin hole carries a hole fit instead.
quote: Designation: Example: Cylindrical pin 10h8×20 IS: 2393 A cylindrical pin of nominal diameter 10mm, tolerance h8 and nominal length 20mm

rule: On a drawing of a pin made to these standards, the surface finish of the pin diameter matches its tolerance: N6 for m6, N7 for h8 and N8 for h11 (taper pins: N6 for type A, N7 for type B).
note: The IS 2393 / IS 6688 finishes are for standard pins; whether PARI's own pin drawings follow them is PARI's call. N-numbers are roughness grade numbers; if PARI writes Ra values, the check needs an N-to-Ra mapping, which isn't printed on these pages. Use for PARI's dowel or locating pins only where they follow these tolerances; the finding is a finish coarser than listed.
quote: Surface finish: N6 for type A and N7 for type B ... N6 dm6ϕ ... N7 dh8ϕ ... N8 dh11ϕ

rule: A keyway for a taper key has the width and the shaft and hub depths (t1, t2) that the IS 2292 table gives for the shaft diameter (e.g. shaft over 30 to 38: 10×8 key, t1 5.0, t2 2.5).
note: adds detail to MC-007. Table covers shafts 6-75 mm. Parallel (feather) keys aren't on these pages. Convert a depth dimensioned as the remaining section (d - t1) before comparing. No keyway width tolerance is given here.
quote: Shaft diameter ... Key width × height ... Keyway depth in shaft t1 ... Keyway depth in hub t2 ... Over 30...38 10×8 5.0 2.5

rule: A Woodruff keyslot has the width, shaft depth t and hub depth t1 that the IS 2294 table gives for the shaft diameter and key (e.g. key 4×5: key diameter 13, t 3.5, t1 1.7).
note: adds detail to MC-007. Table covers shafts over 3 to 17 mm. The figure marks the keyslot's flat bottom as optional.
quote: Designation: Example: Woodruff key 4×5 IS: 2294; a woodruff key of width 4mm and height 5mm

rule: A key is designated by type, width × height (× length for a taper key) and IS number (e.g. 'Taper key 10×8×80 IS: 2292', 'Woodruff key 4×5 IS: 2294'), with a size the table gives for the shaft diameter.
note: adds detail to BM-05. Parts lists; on a shaft drawing the key size may also appear in a keyway note.
quote: Designation: Example: Taper key 10×8×80 IS: 2292; a taper key of width 10mm, height 8mm and length 80mm

rule: A hub keyway for a taper key is drawn and dimensioned with the key's 1:100 taper.
note: adds detail to MC-007. The figure shows the 1:100 taper on the key; the matching hub taper is implied. Judgement is needed to recognise a taper-key hub keyway.
quote: Basic taper 1:100

rule: A key is made of steel with a minimum tensile strength of 58 kgf/mm² (about 570 N/mm²).
note: adds detail to MF-007. Applies only when the drawing is of a key. Needs a material-strength table, which isn't on these pages. kgf/mm² is the book's unit.
quote: Material: Steel with minimum tensile strength 58 kgf/mm²

rule: Where a taper is dimensioned by more than one of ratio 1:x, cone angle, and diameters over a length, the values agree: 1/x = (D - d)/l = 2·tan(α/2).
source_document: Westermann Tables for the Metal Trade (Jutz-Scharkus), revised to Indian Standards; in PARI's WP Specific Guidelines (WESTERMANN_TABLES.pdf, a scan)
supporting_reference: Westermann Tables Taper, Keyways and Chamfers (pdf 71L, book 136)
note: Allow for rounding (the book gives angles to the second). Book misprint: the 1:1.5 cone angle reads 30°52'12'' but its own setting angle 18°26'6'' implies 36°52'12''.
quote: Taper 1:x = (D−d)/l = 2 tan α/2

rule: A taper uses a standard ratio from IS 3458 (1:0.289, 1:0.5, 1:0.866, 1:1.5, 1:3.429, 1:5, 1:6, 1:10, 1:15, 1:20, 1:30, 1:50) or a standard self-holding taper.
source_document: Westermann Tables for the Metal Trade (Jutz-Scharkus), revised to Indian Standards; in PARI's WP Specific Guidelines (WESTERMANN_TABLES.pdf, a scan)
note: A special taper may be intended; warning only. The first three ratios are the 120°, 90° and 60° cones.
quote: Nominal taper 1:x (Ratio of dia D to its axial length K) ... 1:10 5°43'30'' ... (M) taper shaft ends, adj. bearing bushes

rule: A Morse or Metric self-holding taper is called out by its designation (Metric 4, 6, 80; Morse 0 to 6), and any gauge diameter, taper angle or tapped-shank thread shown agrees with IS 1715 (e.g. Morse 3: D 23.825, thread M12).
source_document: Westermann Tables for the Metal Trade (Jutz-Scharkus), revised to Indian Standards; in PARI's WP Specific Guidelines (WESTERMANN_TABLES.pdf, a scan)
note: Covers internal sockets and external shanks, plain and tapped.
quote: Self-holding tapers IS: 1715-1963 ... Designation of taper ... Morse 3 1°26'16'' 5.0 23.825 24.1 19.8 M12

rule: A countersink for a countersunk-head screw has a 90° included angle (60° is the centre-bore angle and 120° the centre-bore countersink).
note: Needs the countersink identified as a screw seat (note or vision).
quote: 1:0.500 90° 45° (M) valve cone, shoulders on piston rod, tip of lathe centre, countersunk screws

rule: A thread undercut has at least the width and radius IS 1369 gives for the thread size, with a diameter no larger than g on an external thread (above M5) and g1 = d + 0.5 mm on an internal thread (e.g. M10 external: width 3.0, radius 1.0, g = d - 2.1).
source_document: Westermann Tables for the Metal Trade (Jutz-Scharkus), revised to Indian Standards; in PARI's WP Specific Guidelines (WESTERMANN_TABLES.pdf, a scan)
source_section: Thread run-out and undercut for ISO threads, IS: 1369-1961 (pdf 52R, book 99)
supporting_reference: related rule MC-003; Westermann Tables Thread run-out and undercut for ISO threads, IS: 1369-1961 (pdf 52R, book 99)
note: Up to M5 the book shows a radiused groove with no g value. The width depends on the chamfer (throat) angle: normal for ≥15°, small for ≥30°.
quote: Width undercut (f) for throat angle α ... Radius r ... Nominal undercut diameter g ... M10, M11 ... 3.0 ... 2.0 1.0 d—2.1

rule: An undercut in an internal ISO thread has a diameter g1 = d + 0.5 mm and at least the width f1 and radius r1 given in IS 1369 for the size (e.g. M10: f1 5.0 normal, r1 1.0).
note: Tabulated from M10 upward.
quote: For internal threads ... Width of undercut (f1) for lead angle α ... Radius r1 ... Normal undercut diameter g1 ... d+0.5

rule: Where an external thread ends at a shoulder without an undercut, the full thread stops at least the run-out X for the size from the shoulder (e.g. M10: 2.5 mm for a normal chamfer).
note: adds detail to MC-003. Needs the thread length and shoulder position from the dimensions. X is the maximum run-out, so the gap must be at least X (M10: 3.5 large, 2.5 normal, 1.6 small).
quote: Runout of threads For bright and semi-bright screws ... Thread Runout X (max) for throat angle α

rule: In a blind tapped hole without an undercut, the drilled depth beyond the full thread allows at least the internal run-out X1 for the size (e.g. normal: M6 2.0, M10 3.0, M20 5.0 mm).
note: adds detail to MC-004. The table also gives a minimum clearance a (normal 2.5 mm for M6-M24) whose position isn't clear in the scan. If it adds to X1, the total is close to IS 4499's S - b1 (WST-226).
quote: Thread runout X1 (max) for lead angle α ... M10, M11 ... 3.0 2.0

rule: A knurl callout states the knurl type (straight, cross or diamond) and the pitch P.
note: adds detail to MX-019. The diamond knurl is drawn at 30° to the axis. The knurled diameter and width are needed too (MX-019).
quote: Pitches for straight, cross and diamond knurling

rule: The knurl pitch is the IS 3403 value for the turned diameter, the knurl width and the material (e.g. diamond knurl on steel, D over 16 to 32, b over 6 to 16: 1.0 mm).
note: adds detail to MX-019. Straight knurling is 'for all materials', cross knurling 'for vulcanite, etc.'
quote: Pitch P for width b ... For light alloys brass fibre, etc. ... For steel ... Over 16 to 32 ... 0.8 1.0 1.0 1.0

rule: The ends of a knurled band are chamfered by about the knurl pitch P.
note: A design reminder taken from one figure; the book states no rule. Shown on the straight-knurling figure only.
quote: Chamfer approx P

rule: A centre-hole callout gives the type (A without, B with a protective chamfer), a standard pilot diameter d1 (1, 1.6, 2.5, 4, 6.3, 10 or 16 mm; type B only up to 6.3) and the standard, e.g. 'Centre Hole A×4 IS: 2473'.
source_document: Westermann Tables for the Metal Trade (Jutz-Scharkus), revised to Indian Standards; in PARI's WP Specific Guidelines (WESTERMANN_TABLES.pdf, a scan)
supporting_reference: related rule MC-009; Westermann Tables Centre Holes, IS: 2473-1963 (pdf 53L, book 100)
note: Type A is a 60° cone without chamfer; type B adds a 120° protective chamfer. A note that forbids centre holes ('CENTER DRILL NOT ALLOWED ON RESTING ...', 2 client PDFs) is not a callout and is not checked.
quote: A centre hole of Type A and diameter, d1=4 mm is designated as Centre Hole A×4 IS: 2473

rule: The centre-hole pilot diameter d1 is a standard size (1, 1.6, 2.5, 4, 6.3, 10 or 16 mm), and type B is used only up to d1 = 6.3.
note: Type B columns are blank for d1 10 and 16.
quote: Dimensions of centre holes in mm ... 10 28 25 22 — — — — —

rule: The centre hole's outer diameter (d2 for type A, d3 for type B) fits within the end face of the shaft it is drilled in.
note: adds detail to MC-009. Shown by the figures, not stated in words. Needs the shaft end diameter (less any end chamfer) from the drawing.
quote: Without chamfer (Type A) ... With chamfer (Type B) ... Type A d1 l1* d2 l2 min Type B l1* b d2 d3 l2 min

rule: If centre holes must not remain on the finished part, the drawing allows the parting-off length l1 for the centre-hole size beyond the finished length (e.g. A×4: 11 mm).
note: adds detail to MC-009. The book has no symbol for 'centre hole permitted / not permitted'; how PARI states this is open.
quote: *Parting off dimension, if the centre hole is to be removed from the finished workpiece.

rule: A clearance (through) hole for a metric bolt or screw has the fine or medium drill diameter from the table for the thread size (e.g. M6: 6.4 fine, 7 medium).
note: adds detail to MC-005. Needs the hole identified as clearance for a given screw size (note or vision). PARI may use a different clearance table; warning only.
quote: Through holes ... For metric threads ... Thread size Fine Medium ... M6 6.4 7

rule: The tap drill stated for a metric tapped hole matches the core-diameter drill for the thread size and material: steel, cast steel or malleable iron (e.g. M10: 8.4) or grey cast iron, brass or bronze (M10: 8.2).
note: adds detail to MC-005. Conflict inside the book: the IS 4499 table (pdf 48R) gives M8 6.75, M10 8.5, M12 10.25 against 6.7, 8.4, 10 here; accept either value or a band covering both, and confirm PARI's tap-drill list. Applies only where the callout states a drill size.
quote: Threaded holes (core diameter d) ... Steel cast steel malleable iron ... Gray cast iron brass bronze ... M10 ... 8.4 8.2
